scope: Exploration and exobiology reference knowledge used by the Mongrels Field Manual and Ask the Mongrels.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Honk every system. The Discovery Scanner is built into every ship, reveals the system's stars and establishes the body count; use the FSS to resolve planets and moons.
details: The Discovery Scanner is integrated into every ship and can be used in normal space or supercruise.
It takes about 5 seconds to charge.
The honk identifies stars and provides the system-wide initial scan; planets and moons still need to be resolved with the Full Spectrum System Scanner or by close proximity.
Exploration data from the initial scan can be sold, but FSS and DSS work increases the information and value you bring home.
commonMistakes: Assuming the honk fully scans every planet in the system.
Leaving a system with an interesting body count without opening the FSS when exploration is the goal.

entries.ruleOfThumb: After the honk, use the FSS to resolve planets, moons and signal sources without flying to each body.
details: The FSS is integrated into every ship.
Use it in supercruise with the ship throttled down, then tune the Filtered Signal Analysis band to the target frequency and zoom in on signals.
The frequency band helps identify the body class before you resolve it, which lets experienced explorers prioritize high-value or interesting targets.
A clear/empty body-frequency bar indicates the system's astronomical bodies have been resolved.
commonMistakes: Flying to every unexplored body before using the FSS.
Ignoring the frequency bar, which can help prioritize what is worth resolving.

sources.name: Elite Dangerous Wiki — Full Spectrum System Scanner

entries.ruleOfThumb: Use the DSS on bodies worth mapping or landing on. It reveals surface points of interest and biological/geological distribution data and adds mapping value.
details: The DSS is an optional internal module used in supercruise and Analysis Mode.
It fires effectively unlimited probes; the module automatically replenishes its small probe clip.
Mapping completes once probe coverage reaches the required surface threshold; the interface rewards efficient probe placement.
For exobiology, DSS mapping is the normal way to reveal selectable biological surface filters before descent.
commonMistakes: Mapping every low-value body automatically instead of choosing targets based on the expedition's goal.
Forgetting to switch to Analysis Mode when trying to use the DSS.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Remember KGBFOAM: O, B, A, F, G, K and M main-sequence stars are scoopable. Route planning that includes scoopable stars is basic deep-space survival.
details: A Fuel Scoop replenishes the main fuel tank while you remain in supercruise near a suitable star.
Scoopable stellar classes are O, B, A, F, G, K and M.
The scoop rate depends on scoop size/quality and proximity to the star; closer is faster but increases heat risk.
A route can still drop you at a non-scoopable primary in a multi-star system, so check the system rather than assuming the arrival star is usable.

quickFacts.label: Scoopable classes
quickFacts.value: O B A F G K M

commonMistakes: Continuing a route without checking the next scoopable star when fuel is low.
Treating maximum scoop rate as more important than safe heat management.

entries.ruleOfThumb: A neutron-star jet-cone supercharge gives one jump at roughly 4x normal range, but it damages the FSD each time. Carry an AFMU if neutron routing is part of the plan.
details: Enter the neutron star's jet cone in supercruise with a Fuel Scoop installed and remain in the cone until the FSD reports that it is supercharged.
A neutron-star supercharge applies a 4x jump-range multiplier to the next hyperspace jump.
Jet-cone boosting damages the FSD, so repeated neutron travel requires module-health management.
White dwarfs can also supercharge an FSD, but provide a much smaller benefit while presenting a comparatively unforgiving exclusion-zone risk; many explorers simply avoid them.
commonMistakes: Entering a jet cone without a working Fuel Scoop.
Using neutron routes repeatedly without an AFMU or watching FSD integrity.
Attempting to scoop inside the exclusion zone rather than remaining in supercruise.

entries.ruleOfThumb: FSD Injection is a one-jump synthesis boost: Basic +25%, Standard +50%, Premium +100%. Save the higher grades for route gaps or emergencies where the extra range matters.
details: FSD Injection is synthesized from raw materials and is labeled FSD Boost on the Galaxy Map.
Basic provides +25% jump range, Standard +50%, and Premium +100% for one hyperspace jump.
FSD Injection does not stack with neutron/white-dwarf supercharging.
Explorers heading toward sparse regions should carry the raw materials before leaving dense space rather than assuming they can gather everything at the edge.
commonMistakes: Using premium injections casually and then lacking the materials when a true route gap appears.
Expecting an injection to stack with a jet-cone supercharge.

entries.ruleOfThumb: An AFMU is the explorer's internal-module repair kit. It can repair most modules, but not the Power Plant, hull, itself, or a canopy that has already fully shattered.
details: The module being repaired is taken offline during the repair and must be re-enabled afterward.
An AFMU cannot repair its own module; carrying two allows them to repair each other.
It cannot repair the Power Plant or hull.
It can repair a damaged canopy before it fully breaks, but cannot restore a canopy after total failure.
Repairing Thrusters or the FSD while in supercruise causes an emergency drop, so conduct repairs safely in normal space.
commonMistakes: Attempting to repair the FSD while still in supercruise.
Assuming an AFMU can restore hull damage.
Waiting until the canopy is completely shattered before trying to repair it.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Treat unsold exploration data as cargo you cannot replace: ship destruction can erase it before turn-in. Survive first; optimize the route second.
details: Discovery, FSS and mapping data can be sold to Universal Cartographics.
Unsold exploration data is lost if the ship is destroyed.
First-discovered and first-mapped credits are tied to successful data turn-in rather than merely visiting the body.
For long expeditions, consider a safe turn-in point before taking unnecessary high-risk detours or combat.
commonMistakes: Taking avoidable combat risks at the end of a long expedition.
Assuming a discovery is permanently credited before the data is sold.

entries.ruleOfThumb: First Footfall is awarded when you are the first CMDR to disembark on an eligible unclaimed body. Unlike first-discovered/mapped data, it is recorded immediately on disembarkation.
details: First Footfall is a planetary-level accolade added with Odyssey.
It is recorded when the first eligible commander disembarks on an unclaimed body; it does not require selling exploration data afterward.
The accolade is independent of whether you later scan biological life on that body.
Inhabited/historically explored bodies are generally not available for new First Footfall credit.

entries.ruleOfThumb: You need an Artemis Suit to perform modern exobiology sampling because it is the suit that carries the Genetic Sampler.
details: The Genetic Sampler is the Artemis Suit's suit-specific tool.
A Detailed Surface Scanner on the ship is strongly recommended because it reveals biological surface filters and makes target selection much faster.
Small ships are often favored for exobiology because they can land closer to organisms in rough terrain.

entries.ruleOfThumb: A complete exobiology specimen requires 3 samples of the same species, each far enough apart to satisfy that organism's clonal-colony range.
details: The first and second scans are partial samples; the third valid scan completes the specimen.
Each genus/species has a clonal-colony range that defines the minimum separation needed for genetic diversity.
If a candidate is too close to the previous sample, the sampler reports insufficient diversity.
Once the third valid sample is collected, the completed specimen is stored for sale to Vista Genomics.
commonMistakes: Taking three scans from a dense cluster without moving far enough between specimens.
Assuming every genus uses the same spacing requirement.

entries.topic: Genetic Sampler: One Species at a Time
entries.ruleOfThumb: Finish all 3 samples of the current species before sampling another one. The Genetic Sampler holds only one in-progress species at a time.
details: Sampling a different species before completing the current set discards the incomplete set.
The sampler's pulse can help distinguish valid, already-sampled and incompatible/different-species targets.
Finish a species before being distracted by another organism nearby; then start the next species.
commonMistakes: Starting a new species with two samples already collected and accidentally throwing away the first set.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Use the sampler's scan pulse while on foot to identify nearby viable specimens and avoid wasting time walking to invalid samples.
details: The Genetic Sampler scan pulse has a reported range of 750 m.
The pulse highlights specimen states with color feedback, helping identify unsampled, already sampled and incompatible targets.
It is especially useful in cluttered terrain where visual identification alone is slow.

entries.ruleOfThumb: After mapping an exobiology body with the DSS, cycle the biological surface filters and descend into terrain where the selected organism is predicted to occur.
details: The DSS overlay is a probability/distribution filter, not a marker showing an exact organism location.
Different genera prefer different terrain, so a broad blue area does not mean every square kilometer will contain visible specimens.
When several biological filters overlap, a landing area can sometimes support multiple organisms and reduce travel time.
commonMistakes: Treating the surface filter like a precise waypoint map.
Remaining in obviously unsuitable terrain just because the overlay is blue.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Completed biological specimens are sold to Vista Genomics, not Universal Cartographics.
details: Vista Genomics purchases completed genetic samples gathered with the Artemis Suit's Genetic Sampler.
Selling biological data pays credits and advances Exobiologist rank.
Keep exploration cartography and exobiology data mentally separate: they use different services and can have different risk/reward priorities on a long expedition.

entries.ruleOfThumb: A First Logged biological sample is exceptionally valuable: current reference tables describe the total payout as 5x the listed base value (base payout plus a 4x bonus).
details: First Logged applies when your completed sample is the first qualifying log for that organism/body context.
The commonly cited current payout is five times the base sample value in total: the normal base payout plus a bonus equal to four additional base payouts.
Because exobiology values have changed historically, treat exact payout tables as living data and re-check them after major Frontier economy updates.
entries.watchFor: Re-check after major exploration/exobiology economy changes because payout multipliers have changed historically.
